title: GIAC GISP
summary: The GIAC Information Security Professional, exam code GISP, is a broad foundation certification from the Global Information Assurance Certification body. GIAC is the certification arm of the SANS Institute, a well known security training organisation. This exam suits security analysts, administrators and managers who need wide coverage of security principles rather than deep work in one tool. Passing it shows an employer that you understand access control, cryptography, business continuity, law and compliance, network security and operations security well enough to talk about them together. The exam is proctored and mixes multiple choice items with performance based questions where you complete tasks in a live environment, and it is open book in the sense that GIAC exams allow you to bring your own printed index. A pass is valid for several years, after which you renew by earning continuing education credits. It leads to roles such as security analyst, security administrator, information security manager or governance and compliance officer. GIAC updates its exams over time, so treat the structure below as the published domain outline and check the vendor current version before you book. This is an independent study guide and it is not approved or sponsored by GIAC or SANS.

beginner.definition: This is a security certification from GIAC, an organisation that tests practical security knowledge. It covers many parts of security instead of one narrow tool. The exam checks that you know the main ideas and can apply them to real situations. It is often chosen by people who want one certificate that shows broad understanding.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security work touches many areas, and this certificate proves you can connect them. Employers read a GIAC pass as a sign of serious study, because GIAC exams are known to be demanding. It supports roles in security operations, administration, audit and management. Because the exam is open book with a printed index, it also rewards good organisation and preparation. It gives you a shared language for talking with technical teams and with managers.
howItWorks: Check the current exam outline on the vendor website and list every domain it names.
Build a study index by topic, because GIAC exams allow a printed reference you made yourself.
Learn the core vocabulary first, such as risk, control, threat, vulnerability and exposure.
Study one domain per week and write your own short explanations instead of copying text.
Practise with the official practice test so you learn the question style before exam day.
Book a proctored session and bring your index, which must follow the vendor rules.
beginner.example: Imagine you must decide whether a payment system that stores card numbers meets its legal duties and is safe. To answer, you combine several ideas at once. You check who can reach the data, which is access control. You check how the numbers are scrambled, which is encryption. You check what happens if the main site goes down, which is continuity planning. You check which law applies, which is compliance. The GISP exam asks questions in that joined up style, so a single fact is rarely enough to pick the right answer.
takeaways: The certification is broad, so plan your study by domain and keep a written index.
You should already work in security or study hard, because the exam assumes basic knowledge.
A pass expires after a set period, so plan to renew it with continuing education credits.

objectives: Describe how access control models protect systems and data.
Explain how cryptography is applied to protect stored and moving information.
Plan for business continuity and disaster recovery in an organisation.
Identify the laws, standards and duties that affect security work.
Outline how networks and telecommunications are secured in practice.
Apply operations security controls to everyday administration tasks.

chapters.title: Access control and cryptography
objectives: Compare access control models and choose one that fits a business need.
Explain how authentication, authorisation and accounting work together.
Apply symmetric and asymmetric encryption to a realistic protection problem.
Explain how hashing and digital signatures prove integrity and origin.
Describe how key management and certificate handling keep trust intact.

chapters.title: Business continuity and disaster recovery
objectives: Identify the critical business functions that must survive a disruption.
Define recovery targets and explain what each one measures.
Choose backup types and test that a restore really works.
Write a continuity plan with clear roles and communication steps.
Review a plan after an incident and improve the weak points.

chapters.title: Legal, regulatory and compliance requirements
objectives: Identify which laws and industry standards apply to a given organisation.
Explain what a security policy is and how it is enforced.
Describe how investigations and evidence handling must be conducted.
Map a control set to a compliance framework and record the evidence.
Explain the privacy duties that apply to personal data.

chapters.title: Network and telecommunications security
objectives: Describe how data moves across a network from sender to receiver.
Recommend controls that protect a network at each layer.
Explain how remote access and wireless links are secured.
Recognise common network attacks and the signs they leave behind.
Choose monitoring and segmentation controls for a given design.

chapters.title: Operations security
objectives: Apply hardening steps to servers, workstations and network devices.
Manage accounts, privileges and changes without breaking service.
Use logging and monitoring to spot abnormal activity early.
Control physical access and media handling in a facility.
Handle incidents in a repeatable and documented way.
